extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematically-literate readers interested in algebraic solution methods for cubic and biquadratic equations (users of geometric constructions, tables of sines, and logarithms)
extracted.subtask_description: Geometric and logarithmic methods for determining the number, signs, bounds, and numerical values of real roots of cubic and biquadratic equations using circle/parabola constructions, tables of (versed) sines, and logarithms. Includes case distinctions depending on coefficient relations and the position of a constructed circle's centre relative to paraboloids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cubic roots: case when centre R falls in space VGP (first formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the centre R, in the first formula of equations, falling in the space VGP, the two intersections YY, fall between A and B, and consequently either of the lesser roots is less than -^b, but the third and greater always exceed -^b, but are exceeded by b.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a geometric criterion linking the locus of the constructed centre R to the signs and comparative bounds of the three roots for the first cubic formula. Use the indicated inequalities (roots relative to -^b and b) to classify the two lesser and the greatest root. (The original notation -^b and b refer to the parameterization used in the construction.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cubic roots: case when centre R in space GNV (first formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: “but if the centre fall in the space GNV, there are two greater than -^b, but less than ^b; and the third is 6 — the two others, and consequently less than -^b.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate placement of R produces a different sign/bounds pattern: two roots between -^b and ^b, and the third less than -^b. Use this to determine which roots are affirmative/negative in the first-formula case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cubic roots: effects of p and q on bounds (general for first/second formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: “using the limitation of the quantity p, the roots are included in narrower bounds; for the greatest root is less than ... but greater than ... ; the middle root is always less than ... but greater than ... ; and the least root never exceeds this limit, but vanishes with the quantity q.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantities p and q tighten bounds on roots: compare p to ^bb (and related expressions) to choose which inequalities apply. When q tends to zero certain roots vanish; when p meets specific thresholds the nature (number/sign) of roots changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cubic roots: case distinctions for second, third, and fourth formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Second formula: “there are two affirmative roots and one negative; and the centre falling in the space GPE, one of the affirmative is greater and the other less than -^b, but the greater does not exceed 6; and the negative cannot be greater than ^i^bb — ^b.” Third & fourth: “in the third formula, there are two negative roots and one affirmative root... the roots are not limited by the quantity b: but the affirmative root is ever less than ... yet greater than ...; and the greatest of the negative is always greater than ... but less than ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each algebraic 'formula' (i.e., sign pattern of coefficients) gives a specific configuration of root signs and bounds depending on the geometric placement of R. Apply the appropriate case rules for the formula in question to deduce which roots are affirmative/negative and their comparative bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to quadratic when centre lies on specific loci
rubrics_metrics.description: “when the centre falls on the line DPD, one of the roots is = 0, and consequently the cubic equation is reduced to a quadratic, or to z^ — bz + p = 0... The equation is also a quadratic, when the centre falls in the axis; that is, when ^g = ^bp — -,\b^ in the first formula, or -^q = -^bbb — ^bp in the second; in the third it is impossible; but in the fourth, when \q = -^^b^ + ^bp.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric positions (centre on line DPD or on axis) correspond to algebraic degeneracies (a root zero or reduction to quadratic). Check these loci to detect and simplify such degenerate cases before further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm: find cubic roots using tables of sines and logarithms (general procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: “by means of a table of sines, the roots of these equations are found... making a division by means of the logarithms... to which answers the angle of 57° 19'... the third part of this is... the sines give the logarithms... which multiplied into the radius produce Y1 & Y2... the roots are 13 — 4 = 9, 13 — 2 = 11, and 13 + 6 = 19...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure summary: compute the relevant radius (from coefficients), form the angle whose tangent (or other trigonometric relation) corresponds to a constructed ratio, take one third of the angle (or of the log depending on presentation), use table of sines/versed sines to obtain factors, multiply by the radius, and combine with ±b to get roots. Use logs to perform multiplications/divisions and obtain cube roots (take one-third of logarithm). Follow the detailed example arithmetic as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using versed sines and logarithms when coefficients are surds or fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: “these roots are readily enough found by means of the logarithmetical table of versed sines; viz. if the coefficients be either surds or fractions, and the roots not to be expressed in numbers, as most commonly is the case. And this is the rule...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coefficients are irrational or fractional so roots are not neat rationals, employ the logarithmetical table of versed sines and log arithmetic to compute necessary cube roots and trigonometric multipliers; follow the provided rule for forming radii and selecting arcs whose versed sines are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed rule for finding cube-root divisor via angle and cosine/versed-sine ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: “in the first and second formulas, if -J-6i be less than p, let ^p — \bb = d, and putting, for the radius, the difference between -^hp and -^b^ + ^q (that is, HR) ... find the angle whose tangent is dV d. Then as the co-sine of that angle is to its versed sine, so the difference, which is taken for radius, to a fourth term; the cube root of which is had by taking 4- of its logarithm. Then dividing 4^p —' ^bb by this cube root, let the divisor be subtracted from the quotient, the remainder will be the quantity Y1; the sum of this remainder and -^b will be the root sought...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this multi-step computational recipe exactly: compute d and radius, find the referenced angle (via tangent), take cosine and versed-sine ratio to form a fourth-term, take logarithm and one-third to get cube root, divide specified expression by cube root, subtract divisor from quotient to get Y1, then add/subtract -^b according to centre-side to obtain the root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biquadratic roots: number of real roots determined by circle centre and radius vs perpendiculars
rubrics_metrics.description: “these [biquadratics] have always either none, or 2, or 4 true roots, the determination of which depends partly on the coefficients, and partly on the sign and magnitude of the absolute number given... a circle from the centre G with the radius ... will intersect the parabola, either in none, or 2, or 4 points; from whence perpendiculars let fall on DH, will give all the roots z. But that they may be 4, it is evident, that the centre of the circle should be found somewhere within a space, from any point of which, three perpendiculars may be let fall upon the curve of the parabola; and also that the radius be less than the greatest of those perpendiculars, and greater than the middle one. But if the centre be posited without this space... then there can be only two roots; but there is none at all, when the radius ... is less than the least...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric test for root count: locate centre G relative to the paraboloids that bound where three perpendiculars exist. If centre inside and radius between middle and greatest perpendicular → 4 real roots. If other placements/radius inequalities hold → 2 or 0 real roots. Use constructed perpendicular lengths as comparators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on last term r for biquadratics found via y-ordinates (use cubic to find y)
rubrics_metrics.description: “As for the limitation of the last term r, it cannot be found with the same ease; because, the letting fall a perpendicular on the curve of a parabola is a solid problem, which cannot be resolved without the solution of a cubic equation... having found those three y, (which are ordinates to the axis of the parabola, from the points where perpendiculars fall on its curve) then 3y* — pyy from the lesser y, will denote the greatest quantity r, if it be — r, than which if r be less, the equation will have four roots, otherwise only two. But if it be -|- r, it should be less than 3y* — pyy from the middle y...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine admissible values of r (which control whether biquadratic has 4,2,0 roots), first solve the auxiliary cubic to get the three y ordinates (perpendiculars). Then compute the specified algebraic combinations (e.g., 3y^2 − p y^2 etc.) from the appropriate y (least, middle, greatest) to obtain bounds on r. Compare r against these bounds to decide root count and sign patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice: remove the second term to simplify biquadratic root classification
rubrics_metrics.description: “because of the perplexing cautions arising from the diversity of signs in these equations, it is always better to take away the second term, and then to seek out the number of roots and the signs, according to the rules already delivered; especially if these quantities are not greatly different from each other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic simplification (depressing the biquadratic by removing the z^3 term) simplifies the geometric analysis and classification of roots. Apply the earlier geometric and cubic-based tests to the depressed equation to determine number and signs of roots more readily.
